# 1. Scientific Question and Data

## Background

Screening for prostate cancer (PCa) is commonly done by taking measures of patients' Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) levels, a relatively low-cost and non-invasive procedure. Although it is widely used for initial diagnoses, it may also be useful in determining further disease progression longitudinally following diagnosis in lieu of more costly and invasive methods.

## Objective and Data Overview

We seek to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of the PSA blood test in determining PCa progression post-diagnosis through sensitivity and specificity analyses conducted on a longitudinal clinical trial sponsored by AstraZeneca (trial NCT00626548). The trial examined the efficacy of ZD4054 (Zibotentan) in treating non-metastatic hormone resistant PCa. The protected-access de-identified data contains information on subject follow-ups throughout the longitudinal study, including longitudinal PSA blood test results and screenings for additional lesions since diagnosis (our proxy for true PCa progression), as well as subject demographic and treatment information. Our measures of interest relate to the joint distribution of event times of first progression as detectable by PSA blood test and screening for new lesions.

## Interval-Censored Longitudinal Data

If a progression event occurs, then it is only known to have occurred between the times of the previous and subsequent visits. Further, if it does not occur before the subject's last follow-up date, then it is known only to have occurred after said date. So our knowledge of each subject's event times is restricted to the (in)finite time intervals in which the true event times exist, i.e. our data is interval-censored.

# 2. Bayesian Model: Latent Hierarchical Joint Log-Normal Regression

Define $Y$ and $Z$ to be the respective latent times of PSA and PCa progression, and $X$ as the $p$-vector of treatment and demographic variables. We posit that

$$
\log\begin{bmatrix}Y\\Z\end{bmatrix}|X,\beta_Y,\beta_Z,\Sigma_{YZ}\sim\mathrm{N}\left(\mu_{YZ},\Sigma_{YZ}\right)
$$

where

$$
\mu_{YZ}=\begin{bmatrix}X^\prime\beta_Y \\
X^\prime\beta_Z\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\Sigma_{YZ}=\begin{bmatrix}
\sigma^2_Y & \sigma_{YZ} \\
\sigma_{YZ} & \sigma^2_Z
\end{bmatrix}
$$

and

$$
\beta_Y,\beta_Z|\beta,\Sigma_\beta\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathrm{N}(\beta,\Sigma_\beta).
$$

We assume that all subjects are independent, but impose no such assumption on each individual's joint distribution of responses $Y,Z$ so that the latent health/disease progression can jointly drive the PSA and PCa progression event times, quantified by the covariance parameter $\sigma_{YZ}$. The joint hierarchical specification of $\beta_Y,\beta_Z$ is motivated by the knowledge that both PSA and PCa progression should be roughly symmetrically affected by the treatment and demographic covariates, encouraging an informative, near-zero concentrated prior on the entries of $\Sigma_\beta$.

## Conditional Data Likelihood

For $i=1,\cdots,n$ independent subjects, we observe data $(x,y^L,y^R,z^L,z^R)_i$ where $y^L$ and $y^R$ and the left and right endpoints of the event time intervals for $Y$, and $z^L$ and $z^R$ are the analogous interval endpoints of $Z$. The resulting data likelihood for the latent outcome pair is

$$
\begin{aligned}
p((y^L_i,y^R_i,z^L_i,z^R_i)_{i=1,\cdots,n}|X,\beta_Y,\beta_Z,\Sigma_{YZ})&=\prod_{i=1}^n\mathbb{P}\left(y^L_i<Y<y^R_i,z^L_i<Z<z^R_i|X=x_i\right) \\
&=\prod_{i=1}^n\int_{\log y^L_i}^{\log y^R_i}\int_{\log z^L_i}^{\log z^R_i}\phi(s_Y(u),s_Z(v);\rho)\,dv\,du \\
&=\prod_{i=1}^n\Big\lbrack\Phi(s_Y(\log y^R_i),s_Z(\log z^R_i);\rho)-\Phi(s_Y(\log y^R_i),s_Z(\log z^L_i);\rho) \\
&\qquad{}-\Phi(s_Y(\log y^L_i),s_Z(\log z^R_i);\rho)+\Phi(s_Y(\log y^L_i),s_Z(\log z^L_i);\rho)\Big\rbrack \\
\end{aligned}
$$

where $s_A(a)=(a-x_i^\prime\beta_A)/\sigma_A$ standardizes its argument, $\rho=\sigma_{YZ}/(\sigma_Y\sigma_Z)$ is the co-pathway outcomes' correlation, and $\phi(a,b;\rho)$ and $\Phi(a,b;\rho)$ are the standard bivariate normal distribution's PDF and CDF with correlation $\rho$, respectively. The log-normal likelihood is used as it has a strictly non-negative support and an increasing variance as the location parameter increases, which are common assumptions in survival analysis.

## Analysis Outcome Measures

Given posterior draws for $\beta_Y,\sigma^2_Y,\beta_Z,\sigma^2_Z$, the posterior predictive distributions $Y^*|X^*,Y,X$ and $Z^*|X^*,Z,X$ can be estimated for an individual with treatment/demographics $X^*$. The confusion matrix

|                    |                                    |                                    |
|-------------------:|-----------------------------------:|-----------------------------------:|
|                    |                 No PSA Progression |                    PSA Progression |
| No PCa Progression | $=\mathbb{P}(Y^*>t,Z^*>t|X^*,Y,X)$ | $=\mathbb{P}(Y^*<t,Z^*>t|X^*,Y,X)$ |
|    PCa Progression | $=\mathbb{P}(Y^*>t,Z^*<t|X^*,Y,X)$ | $=\mathbb{P}(Y^*<t,Z^*<t|X^*,Y,X)$ |
|                    |                                    |                                    |

can be used to assess the diagnostic accuracy of PSA in predicting PCa progression at various clinical horizons $t$ and subject treatments/demographics $X$. We focus on the one-year $(t=365)$ horizon and assess subjects of various treatment/demographics combinations.

The posterior distribution of $\rho=\sigma_{YZ}/(\sigma_Y\sigma_Z)$ quantifies the strength of the co-pathway relationship between PSA and PCa progression. We examine this posterior as a heuristic to support the contingency table analysis.

# 3. Prior Distributions

Recall our hierarchical joint specification $\beta_Y,\beta_Z|\beta,\Sigma_\beta\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathrm{N}(\beta,\Sigma_\beta)$ for the relationship between subject covariates and the latent co-pathway outcomes $Y,Z$. To encourage closeness between $\beta_Y$ and $\beta_Z$ in parameter space, we use the conjugate prior $(\Sigma_\beta)_{j,j}^{-1}\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathrm{Gamma}(a_0,b_0)$ for $j=1,\cdots,p$ on the precision of each coefficient's difference from the corresponding entry in the latent vector $\beta$. The off-diagonal entries are set to 0 as a simplifying assumption. The conjugate $\beta_j\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathrm{N}(m_0, v_0)$, $j=1,\cdots,p$ prior is used for the latent co-pathway demographics-related progression drivers. We consider hyperparameter assignments $a_0=2$, $b_0=1$, $m_0=0$, and $v_0=1000$ as our defaults to encourage small $\Sigma_\beta$ (higher concentration of $\beta_Y,\beta_Z$ around the global $\beta$) and a non-informative $\beta$ prior.

To jointly model the latent time-to-event outcome covariance matrix $\Sigma_{YZ}$, we use the $(\Sigma_{YZ})^{-1}\sim\mathrm{Wishart}(d_0, W_0)$ conjugate prior on the precision matrix with general-use default hyperparameter assignments of $d_0=2$ and $W_0=I_2/2$, which is the least informative proper Wishart prior, and has expectation $I_2$.

The specific choices of default hyperparameters were chosen by a short simulation study conducted prior to the analysis of real data.

# 4. Posterior Computation and Diagnostics

The joint posterior is defined up to a normalizing constant below.

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\pi(\beta_Y,\beta_Z,\beta,\Sigma_{YZ},\Sigma_\beta|y^L_i,y^R_i,z^L_i,z^R_i) \\
\propto&p((y^L_i,y^R_i,z^L_i,z^R_i)_{i=1,\cdots,n}|X,\beta_Y,\beta_Z,\Sigma_{YZ})\times\pi(\beta_Y,\beta_Z|\beta,\Sigma_\beta)\times\pi(\beta)\times\pi(\Sigma_{YZ})\times\pi(\Sigma_\beta) \\
\propto&\prod_{i=1}^n\Big\lbrack\Phi(s_Y(\log y^R_i),s_Z(\log z^R_i);\rho)-\Phi(s_Y(\log y^R_i),s_Z(\log z^L_i);\rho) \\
&\qquad{}-\Phi(s_Y(\log y^L_i),s_Z(\log z^R_i);\rho)+\Phi(s_Y(\log y^L_i),s_Z(\log z^L_i);\rho)\Big\rbrack \\
&\times\det(\Sigma_\beta)^{-1}\exp\left\{-\dfrac{1}{2}\left\lbrack(\beta_Y-\beta)^\prime\Sigma_\beta^{-1}(\beta_Y-\beta)+(\beta_Z-\beta)^\prime\Sigma_\beta^{-1}(\beta_Z-\beta)\right\rbrack\right\} \\
&\times\exp\left\{-\dfrac{1}{2}(\beta-m_01_p)^\prime v_0^{-1}I_p(\beta-m_01_p)\right\} \\
&\times\det(\Sigma_{YZ})^{1/2}\exp\{-\text{tr}(2I_2\Sigma_{YZ}^{-1})/2\} \\
&\times\left\lbrack\prod_{j=1}^p\left(\Sigma_\beta^{-1}\right)_{j,j}\right\rbrack^{\alpha_0-1}\exp\left\{-b_0\times\text{tr}\left(\Sigma_\beta^{-1}\right)\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

Due to the inherent interval-censored outcomes, the posterior is improper and must be sampled from using Metropolis-Hastings and Gibbs sampling techniques. We utilize the R package `rjags` to specify and cyclically extract draws from the full conditional posterior.

It should be noted that to improve posterior stability in the right-censored cases, the observed upper bounds are set to the minimum of the factual upper bounds and 2000. Similarly, the lower bounds are the minimum of the factual lower bound and 1000.

Through repeated experimentation, we settle on computing 4 chains each with 2500 posterior draws following a thinning rate of 4 and 1000 burn-in draws to balance computation time, convergence testing capability, effective sample size, and memory usage.

# 7. Alternative Analysis, Comparison, and Bayesian Justification

## Alternative Model

### Model: Hierarchical Gamma Model around a Common Latent Progression Time

To assess whether our conclusions depend on the log-normal assumption and on the form of the dependence between outcomes, we fit an alternative model that is built around a common latent progression time. With $Y$, $Z$, and $X$ defined as in Section 2, let $T$ be a subject-level latent progression event time. We posit

$$
  \begin{aligned}
T\mid X,\beta,\alpha_T&\sim\mathrm{Gamma}\left(\alpha_T,\ \alpha_T e^{-X^\prime\beta}\right), \\
Y\mid T,\alpha_Y&\sim\mathrm{Gamma}\left(\alpha_Y,\ \alpha_Y/T\right), \\
Z\mid T,\delta,\alpha_Z&\sim\mathrm{Gamma}\left(\alpha_Z,\ \alpha_Z/(e^{\delta}T)\right),
\end{aligned}
$$
  
  where the gamma distributions are parameterized by shape and rate, and $Y$ and $Z$ are conditionally independent given $T$. Under this specification

$$
  \mathbb{E}[T\mid X]=e^{X^\prime\beta},
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T]=T,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[Z\mid T]=e^{\delta}T,
$$
  
  so the latent progression time $T$ carries all of the covariate information, and the PSA and PCa progression times scatter around it. Equivalently, on the log scale,

$$
  \log Y=X^\prime\beta+\log\varepsilon_T+\log\varepsilon_Y,
\qquad
\log Z=X^\prime\beta+\delta+\log\varepsilon_T+\log\varepsilon_Z,
$$
  
  with independent $\varepsilon_A\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_A,\alpha_A)$ for $A\in\{T,Y,Z\}$.

This formulation imposes the conditional dependence between $Y$ and $Z$ given $X$ directly, through the shared latent time, rather than through a covariance parameter. It represents the latent health and disease progression motivated in Section 2 as an explicit event time: a subject whose underlying disease progresses late tends to show late PSA progression and late PCa progression. The implied covariance of the log event times given $X$ is

$$
  \mathrm{Cov}\left(\begin{bmatrix}\log Y\\\log Z\end{bmatrix}\Big|X\right)=
  \begin{bmatrix}
\psi_1(\alpha_T)+\psi_1(\alpha_Y) & \psi_1(\alpha_T) \\
\psi_1(\alpha_T) & \psi_1(\alpha_T)+\psi_1(\alpha_Z)
\end{bmatrix},
$$
  
  where $\psi_1$ is the trigamma function, so that $\mathrm{Var}(\log\varepsilon_A)=\psi_1(\alpha_A)$. The co-pathway correlation

$$
  \rho=\frac{\psi_1(\alpha_T)}{\sqrt{\left(\psi_1(\alpha_T)+\psi_1(\alpha_Y)\right)\left(\psi_1(\alpha_T)+\psi_1(\alpha_Z)\right)}}
$$
  
  is the correlation of the log event times, the same quantity as $\rho=\sigma_{YZ}/(\sigma_Y\sigma_Z)$ in the primary model, so the two can be compared directly. It is large when variation in the latent progression time dominates the outcome-specific scatter around it, and it is restricted to $(0,1)$. A non-negative association is clinically reasonable, since a common disease process should delay or accelerate both types of progression together. It can be checked against the posterior of $\rho$ under the primary model, which is unrestricted.

#### Shared covariate effects

Because covariates enter only through $T$, the alternative model replaces the primary model's hierarchical prior $\beta_Y,\beta_Z\mid\beta,\Sigma_\beta\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathrm{N}(\beta,\Sigma_\beta)$ with a single coefficient vector $\beta$. Each covariate therefore has the same multiplicative effect on PSA and PCa progression: $\exp(\beta_j)$ is the time ratio associated with a unit change in $X_j$ for $T$, $Y$, and $Z$ alike. The primary model's hierarchical prior was motivated by the expectation that both outcomes are roughly symmetrically affected by the treatment and demographic covariates. The alternative model makes that expectation exact, and it plays the role of the limiting case $\Sigma_\beta\to0$, apart from the outcome-specific offset $\delta$.

This is a stronger conditional distribution assumption on $Y,Z\mid X$, and it is the main way the alternative model departs from the primary one. It removes $p$ regression parameters and the hierarchical variance parameters. The cost is that a covariate acting on one outcome more than the other cannot be represented. For example, anti-androgen therapy acts directly on PSA production, and bisphosphonates act on bone, where radiographic metastases are commonly detected. If such effects were substantial, the shared $\beta$ would average them across the two outcomes. We assess this by comparing the alternative model's $\beta$ with the primary model's posteriors for $\beta_Y$ and $\beta_Z$.

NEED comparison of $\beta$ with the primary model's $\beta_Y$ and $\beta_Z$

#### Offset between outcomes

The parameter $\delta$ allows PCa progression to occur systematically later (or earlier) than PSA progression for a given latent progression time, with $e^{\delta}=\mathbb{E}[Z\mid T]/\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T]$. Without it, the model would force both outcomes to occur at the same time on average, which is implausible given that rising PSA typically precedes radiographic evidence of progression. Only one offset is identifiable alongside the intercept in $\beta$, so $Y$ is centered on $T$ and the offset is placed on $Z$.

#### Choice of the gamma distribution

The gamma distribution shares the two properties used to motivate the log-normal likelihood in Section 2: strictly positive support, and variance that increases with the location, here with a constant coefficient of variation $\alpha_A^{-1/2}$. Both models are accelerated failure time models, in which covariates act multiplicatively on the event time, so covariate effects are on the same time-ratio scale. The intercepts are not directly comparable, since $\mathbb{E}[\log Y\mid X]=X^\prime\beta+\sum_{A\in\{T,Y\}}\left(\psi(\alpha_A)-\log\alpha_A\right)$ under this model, where $\psi$ is the digamma function.

The gamma and log-normal distributions differ in hazard shape and tails. The log-normal hazard is non-monotone: it rises to a peak and then declines, with a heavy right tail. The gamma hazard at each level of the model is monotone: increasing for $\alpha_A>1$, decreasing for $\alpha_A<1$, and constant (exponential) for $\alpha_A=1$. The log-gamma errors are also left-skewed on the log-time scale, which places relatively more mass on early event times than symmetric normal errors. Marginally over $T$, each observed event time is a product of two independent gamma variables rather than a gamma variable. Because the one-year progression status of subjects with incomplete follow-up is recovered from the model, a different shape over the first 365 days is precisely the kind of assumption that could alter the estimated confusion matrix. Agreement between the two models would indicate that the diagnostic accuracy conclusions are robust to both the choice of event-time distribution and the form of the dependence between outcomes.

### Conditional Data Likelihood

The observed data $(x,y^L,y^R,z^L,z^R)_i$, $i=1,\cdots,n$, are as in Section 2. Because $Y$ and $Z$ are conditionally independent given $T$, the likelihood factorizes given the latent progression times $t=(t_1,\cdots,t_n)$:
  
  $$
  \begin{aligned}
&p((y^L_i,y^R_i,z^L_i,z^R_i)_{i=1,\cdots,n}\mid t,\delta,\alpha_Y,\alpha_Z) \\
&\qquad=\prod_{i=1}^n\Big\lbrack F_Y(y^R_i\mid t_i)-F_Y(y^L_i\mid t_i)\Big\rbrack\Big\lbrack F_Z(z^R_i\mid t_i)-F_Z(z^L_i\mid t_i)\Big\rbrack,
\end{aligned}
$$
  
  where $F_Y(\cdot\mid t_i)$ is the gamma CDF with shape $\alpha_Y$ and rate $\alpha_Y/t_i$, $F_Z(\cdot\mid t_i)$ is the gamma CDF with shape $\alpha_Z$ and rate $\alpha_Z/(e^{\delta}t_i)$, and $F_A(0\mid t_i)=0$. The marginal likelihood integrates each subject's term over $t_i\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_T,\alpha_T e^{-x_i^\prime\beta})$. In place of the bivariate normal CDF of the primary model, the dependence between outcomes enters through the shared $t_i$.

### Analysis Outcome Measures

The outcome measures are unchanged from Section 2. For each posterior draw of $(\beta,\delta,\alpha_T,\alpha_Y,\alpha_Z)$, a posterior predictive pair for a subject with covariates $X^*$ is generated by drawing $T^*\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_T,\alpha_T e^{-X^{*\prime}\beta})$, and then $Y^*\mid T^*$ and $Z^*\mid T^*$ independently from their gamma distributions. The confusion matrix of Section 2 is estimated at the one-year horizon $t=365$, from which

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{sensitivity}&=\mathbb{P}(Y^*<t\mid Z^*<t,X^*,Y,X), \\
\text{specificity}&=\mathbb{P}(Y^*>t\mid Z^*>t,X^*,Y,X).
\end{aligned}
$$

As in the primary model, the posterior distribution of $\rho$ is examined as a heuristic to support the contingency table analysis.

### Prior Distributions

With a single coefficient vector, no hierarchical prior is needed. We use the same non-informative prior as the primary model's global coefficients,

$$
  \beta_j\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathrm{N}(m_0,v_0),\quad j=1,\cdots,p,
\qquad
\delta\sim\mathrm{N}(0,v_0),
$$
  
  with $m_0=0$ and $v_0=1000$. The Wishart prior on $\Sigma_{YZ}$ is replaced by priors on the three gamma shapes, which together determine the log-time covariance:
  
  $$
  \alpha_T,\alpha_Y,\alpha_Z\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathrm{Gamma}(s_0,r_0),\qquad s_0=2,\ r_0=1.
$$
  
  This prior has its mode at $\alpha_A=1$ (the exponential model), mean 2, and central 95% interval $(0.24,5.57)$. It covers decreasing, constant, and increasing hazards, and coefficients of variation between roughly 0.42 and 2.03, without favoring either hazard direction.

### Posterior Computation and Diagnostics

The joint posterior, including the latent progression times $t$, is defined up to a normalizing constant by

$$
  \begin{aligned}
&\pi(\beta,\delta,\alpha_T,\alpha_Y,\alpha_Z,t\mid y^L_i,y^R_i,z^L_i,z^R_i) \\
\propto&\prod_{i=1}^n\Big\lbrack F_Y(y^R_i\mid t_i)-F_Y(y^L_i\mid t_i)\Big\rbrack\Big\lbrack F_Z(z^R_i\mid t_i)-F_Z(z^L_i\mid t_i)\Big\rbrack \\
&\times\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{(\alpha_T e^{-x_i^\prime\beta})^{\alpha_T}}{\Gamma(\alpha_T)}t_i^{\alpha_T-1}\exp\left\{-\alpha_T e^{-x_i^\prime\beta}t_i\right\} \\
&\times\exp\left\{-\dfrac{1}{2v_0}\left\lbrack(\beta-m_01_p)^\prime(\beta-m_01_p)+\delta^2\right\rbrack\right\} \\
&\times(\alpha_T\alpha_Y\alpha_Z)^{s_0-1}\exp\{-r_0(\alpha_T+\alpha_Y+\alpha_Z)\}.
\end{aligned}
$$
  
  As with the primary model, we sample from the posterior using `rjags`, with the interval-censored event times and the latent progression times treated as latent variables, and the event times constrained to their observed intervals. For comparability, the alternative model uses the same data handling as Section 4: upper bounds are set to the minimum of the factual upper bound and 2000, and lower bounds to the minimum of the factual lower bound and 1000. The MCMC settings also match the primary model: 4 chains, each with 1000 burn-in iterations and 2500 retained draws at a thinning rate of 4, for 10,000 posterior draws in total. Posterior draws of $\rho$ and of the log-time covariance matrix are computed from the draws of $\alpha_T$, $\alpha_Y$, and $\alpha_Z$.

The three shape parameters are separated only through how the two outcomes vary jointly around the latent progression time, so they may mix more slowly than $\beta$ and $\delta$. We therefore examine their diagnostics first, and lengthen the chains if they do not meet the convergence criterion.

Convergence is assessed with the same `posterior_diagnostics()` function used for the primary model. It produces trace plots and autocorrelation plots for each parameter, the Gelman–Rubin potential scale reduction factor $\hat R$ (target $\hat R<1.1$), the effective sample size, and the Monte Carlo standard error.

## Model Comparisons

## Bayesian Justification

We are motivated towards a Bayesian approach due to three primary characteristics of our research objective.

First, our data is inherently interval-censored, which makes it desirable for us to incorporate uncertainty induced by the reduced data information into our parameter estimation. Frequentist estimators would not be able to incorporate parameter uncertainty as elegantly in this context.

Second, the recovery of the joint conditional time-to-event outcomes is required for our study outcome measures. The Bayesian approach nicely facilitates this with appropriate uncertainty quantification by simulation from the posterior predictive distribution.

Third, our desire to incorporate assumptions about the common effects of demographic and cancer treatment information on the co-pathway outcomes into the model requires a hierarchical formulation of the regression parameter distributions, an approach that is exclusive to the Bayesian philosophy.

## Simulation Study

To illustrate the advantages of our Bayesian approach, we consider a competing Frequentist approach in a simulation study where the true sample event times are known.

The competing frequentist model is

$$
\log\begin{bmatrix}Y\\Z\end{bmatrix}|x\sim\mathrm{N}_2\left(\begin{bmatrix}\beta_Y^\prime\\ \beta_Z^\prime\end{bmatrix}x,\text{diag}(\sigma^2_Y,\sigma^2_Z)\right)
$$

which is equivalent to two independent linear regressions of the latent outcomes $\log(Y)$ and $\log(Z)$ on $x$.

For each simulation, we sample $n=600$ realizations of the $p=10$-vector $x_i\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathrm{N}_p(\vec 0_p,v_0I_p)|_{i=1,\cdots,n}$. Denote the full data covariates $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$. Fix $\beta=(\beta_j)^\prime_{j=1,\cdots,p}$ where $\beta_j=(-1)^{\mathbb{I}(j\leq p/2)}$. We draw assignments $\beta_Y,\beta_Z\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathrm{N}_p(\beta,\Sigma_\beta)$. Latent log-event times $(\log Y, \log Z)_i^\prime$ are jointly drawn from $\mathrm{N}_2(5+x_i^\prime\begin{bmatrix}\beta_Y,\beta_Z\end{bmatrix}, \Sigma_{YZ})$. Observed lower event-time interval bounds are $y^L_i=\min\{100\lfloor Y_i/100\rfloor,500\}$, and upper bounds are $y^R_i=\min\{a\in\{100,200,300,400,500,2000\}|a\geq\min\{Y,2000\}\}$. $z^L_i$ and $z^R_i$ are assigned symmetrically. The resulting observed data used by the examined methods per-simulation is $(X,y^L_i,y^R_i,z^L_i,z^R_i)$.

The Bayesian methods are performed on the data as described earlier in the text, with the exception of running a single chain of length 1000 with no thinning instead of 4 of length 2500 with a thinning rate of 4. This was done to ease the computational burden under repeated simulation, and we find no issues with posterior convergence under these MCMC parameters. The Frequentist approach optimizes its respective likelihood (which is withheld due to being largely analogous with the Bayesian data likelihood) with respect to parameters $\beta_Y,\beta_Z,\sigma^2_Y,\sigma^2_Z$, implemented using the `survival` package. All models include an intercept term to capture the event time offset included in the simulation procedure.

The frequentist approach returns fitted values for the latent $Y,Z$ pair per sample, and we use the exponential of the log-posterior predictive distribution mean as the Bayesian point estimate for the latent outcomes. Exponentiating the log-scale mean is far more numerically stable than using the mean of the raw posterior predictive distribution, and in line with common survival analysis practice. Methods are compared by the root mean squared difference between estimated and actual log-event times for $Y$ and $Z$, analogous to RMSE on the log-time-to-event scale.

We perform 50 simulation replications under parameters $v_o=1$, $\Sigma_\beta=I_p/4$, and $\Sigma_{YZ}=((2,1)^\prime,(1,2)^\prime)$. The results are presented in terms of per-simulation error comparisons between the three methods.

# 8. Innovation or Extension

Our innovations can be found in our implementation of a hierarchical regression model and modeling of the latent disease-driven co-pathway outcomes after controlling for covariates. These decisions arise from our assumed relationship between $Y$ and $Z$ in terms of their relationships with $X$ and further correlation after controlling for $X$.

## Hierarchical Regression

We impose a hierarchical structure on the regression parameter vectors to perform partial regularization towards the mean covariate effect, and to share information between the outcomes in quantifying the effects of $X$. To our knowledge, this particular application of hierarchical modeling has not been considered as a widespread procedure for sharing information between outcomes and is novel in our setting.

## Latent Disease-Driven Co-pathway Outcomes

Although demographic- and treatment-related information is captured in the regression on $X$, we posit that the disease information is not. Further, we assume that the latent disease information jointly drives $Y$ and $Z$. In lieu of observable features to jointly regress upon, we instead assume that there exists a partial correlation structure between $Y$ and $Z$ given $X$. Our choice of bivariate lognormal conditional distribution for the $Y,Z$ pair naturally facilitates modeling the partial covariance between $Y,Z|X$.

# References
